title: Wadi: design and customize a Konkan house with your AI agent
pitch: Structurally sound homes for families who couldn't afford an architect: an agent codes a Konkan home into a 3D model contractors build from, and owners customize it by chatting with a WebMCP agent.
about_excerpt: Structurally sound homes for families who couldn't afford an architect: an agent codes a Konkan home into a 3D model contractors build from, and owners customize it by chatting with a WebMCP agent. Like 7 Comment 7 Story Updates 2 Opening screen of Wadi showing pre-designed models that the user can choose and modify using the AI agent A fully loaded model that is generated from the design language code that was written by an architect with the help of a coding agent The design language code editor that a trained architect can create or modify directly or with a coding agent A graph of the rooms and connections between them that forms part of the structural constraints that ground the AI agents A detailed diagram of a hip roof construction that is automatically generated Floor plans are also automatically generated Elevation views are generated automatically as well Bill of materials for all of the construction (WIP) Actual house and Wadi 3D model view based on which the house is being constructed Actual house and Wadi 3D model view based on which the house is being constructed Actual house and Wadi 3D model view based on which the house is being constructed Actual house and Wadi 3D model view based on which the house is being constructed Inspiration In the Konkan (coastal region of the state of Maharashtra in India), many families build their homes with government housing grants. The grant covers construction, but not an architect, so the design falls to the local contractor and mason, who lay out the house room by room from experience. The owner rarely sees what their home will look like until it is standing. Wadi is built for exactly this gap. It is a parametric home designer that produces a full 3D model, dimensioned floor plans, elevations, and a roof, from designs that already follow the standard local materials and construction of the region: the laterite walls, Mangalore tiled hip roof, the raised plinth, the verandah on pillars. A homeowner can walk through their house in 3D before a single brick is laid. A contractor can start from a standard layout or sketch their own, and then refine it, without being a trained architect. That last part is where agents come in, and Wadi uses them for two different people. An architect (or a coding agent acting as one) designs a full house from scratch through Wadi's offline MCP server, authoring the complete model in Wadi's own design language, checked against structural rules at every step. Then the family customizes that design in their own browser through WebMCP. A 3D design tool is hostile to an agent: the scene lives in a <canvas> invisible to the accessibility tree, so the agent is left guessing at buttons. WebMCP fixes that. The site exposes structured design tools the agent calls directly, so a homeowner or contractor can start from a finished local design and just describe changes in plain language, "add a pooja room off the hall, widen the verandah, put the staircase here", while the agent makes real, sound edits and the family watches the model update. What it does Wadi separates the two people who touch a design, over one model and one design language. An architect designs the full house from scratch through Wadi's offline MCP server. Running inside a coding agent (Claude Code, or any MCP client), the architect authors the complete model in Wadi's .wdl design language, adding floors, rooms, a roof, and a staircase, checking each version against the structural rules and previewing the plans, elevations, and roof, all without the app. The family then customizes that design in the browser , through WebMCP and a hosted online MCP server, with nothing to install. The homeowner or contractor opens the app, picks the local design closest to what they want, and talks to an in-browser agent (ChatGPT's built-in browser, or Chrome). The agent reads the design, edits it, resize a room, add a bathroom, change the plot, and applies it, and the person watches the 3D model, floor plans, and roof re-flow live. Because a design is a parametric model, changing one number re-flows the whole house. Both go through the same store the person edits by hand, so agent edits and human edits are the same kind of change, on one live model with one undo history: you can talk a house into shape and then hand-tune it. A live co-editing relay even lets a remote agent edit the model a family is watching, in real time. How we built it The core is a Zod HouseConfig schema, a parametric resolver, and a geometry expander. Any number in the model can be a formula over named variables, points, and guide lines, so the whole house re-flows when one value changes. A generated guide, for example, resolves lazily by index: $$\text{module}.x_i = o_x + i \cdot s_x$$ Every mutation runs through a Zustand store that re-resolves the parametric model, so the 2D and 3D renderers always read resolved numbers. The edit surface is Wadi's .wdl design language , a small language for a whole house (floors, rooms, walls, roofs, variables, formulas), compiled through the real pipeline. Making the DSL the single edit surface was the key decision: an agent reads the current house with get_wdl , edits the text, and applies it with set_wdl , which compiles it, loads it into the same store the UI uses, and returns a structural check. So the agent is not a second app driving Wadi from outside, it is another hand on the same model. Because the person customizing is not an architect , that same set_wdl runs a structural constraint linter on every edit, a growing set of rules that keep a spoken change buildable: a plinth on the lowest floor, a roof on the highest, the roof covering the whole top floor, pillars under any cantilever, upper-floor walls aligned over the walls below, plus checks on slabs, floor heights, openings, room overlaps, and passable connections. Each returns a plain-language warning the agent must resolve, so a change from someone with no design training still lands a real, buildable house. Two MCP surfaces sit on this core. The offline MCP server gives an architect the from-scratch design tools inside their own coding agent ( wadi_check , wadi_preview , wadi_reference , wadi_examples ); it predates the hackathon. During the hackathon we built the end-user side: a hosted online MCP server (a Cloudflare Container at mcp.wadi.house ) so a family's agent (Antigravity, a ChatGPT connector, Gemini) reaches the tools by URL with nothing installed, and the WebMCP layer , which registers the editing tools in the browser with document.modelContext.registerTool ( get_wdl , set_wdl , check , list_homes , choose_home , capture_view , undo / redo ) so an in-browser agent drives the live model. A Durable-Object relay bridges the two, letting a remote agent co-edit the very model a user is watching. video_transcript_excerpt: Wadi an app that allows you to design and customize a typical Konkan house with your AI agent. Let's see how Wadi actually works. It uses a domain-specific language that generates the entire model of the house. An architect can learn the language and type the code or use a coding agent to generate the model. The code can be shared with anyone and they can open the file to generate the 3D model and explore it. The app works fully offline in a mobile app or in a browser. What we have built now is a very exciting capability using a technology called WebMCP where an untrained contractor can make changes to the model just by using conversations. >> The tiny one-bedroom home is loaded. One bed, bath, kitchen, living room, front porch, and rear terrace. What would you like to change first? >> I have hidden the roof to see how the layout looks from inside. I think the kitchen is too cramped. >> The kitchen is about 8 and 1/2 by 7 and 3/4 ft and the bathroom is about 8 and 1/2 by 8. I'd propose extending the house 4 ft north-south, keeping the bathroom as is, and giving all four added feet to the kitchen with the bedroom and living room also getting 4 ft deeper. Want me to apply that? Okay, I'll adjust that proposal. Done. The kitchen is now about 8 and 1/2 by 10 and 3/4 ft. The bathroom is unchanged and the bedroom and living room are each 3 ft deeper. >> Now let's do one thing. If we can repeat the same layout in another floor on top >> Let me check that setup. I can duplicate the whole layout directly above and close the upper porch's south edge with a protective wall. One question, where should the staircase go? External beside the porch or internal taking space from the living room? >> We'll work on the staircase later. Just add the top floor and let me see how it looks. >> Sure, I'll set that up. The upper floor is in place and the upper porch has a south wall. The roof has no divider and there's no staircase yet. >> Okay, now add a staircase to the east side of the house in a north-south direction. >> Got it. I'll plan that. The first stair layout is in place, but the landing ended up at the front. So, I'm correcting that. >> We are here in a village of Atali where our project Gamino is being conducted. Homes in the village are built with mud and clay tiles like this. The government has sanctioned funds to allow villagers to reconstruct their homes using local laterite stone and Mangalore tiles. However, the structural integrity of these homes is left to inexperienced contractors. It is for people like this who cannot afford an architect that Wadi has been specifically designed for.

live_observation.first_impression: Landing page clearly presents Wadi as a house-design tool for families, with a prominent route into a browser designer.
live_observation.action_attempted: Opened the designer and viewed the home chooser.
live_observation.after_state: The designer loaded with home templates, filters, 3D Model/Floor Plans/Elevations/Roof Details tabs, and save/open controls.
live_observation.notes: The chooser exposes Konkan and Hip roof filters plus parametric home templates; a structural warnings indicator showed 9 warnings.
